microbooks.title: Streetlight Math
microbooks.when: Phoenix, a few weeks before the knock on the window that opens HUNTED
microbooks.setting_mood: parking lot at night, counting, a sedan with its lights off
microbooks.logline: Ryan Kane parks under the third streetlight, counts nine lights, and watches a dark sedan that will not leave.
microbooks.canon_notes: Uses only established HUNTED details: the 2007 Civic, sleeping bag and garbage bags in back, Emma's number he never calls, his father's watch, the VA breathing technique, the TBI and the counting habit ("Count. Measure. Document."). Set before Chapter 1, when Ryan had already been living in the car for weeks. Adds nothing about Skull or later events.
microbooks.label: Original companion fiction set in the world of the Ryan Kane Series. Not an excerpt from any book.
microbooks.text:
I parked under the third streetlight because the first two buzzed.

That was the rule I made that night. I made a new rule most nights. Rules were easier than plans. A plan needed a tomorrow, and I wasn't sure I had one of those. A rule only needed the next ten minutes.

The lot belonged to a strip mall that had given up. A nail salon with paper over the windows. A tax place. A sandwich shop that closed at nine and left its neon OPEN sign burning anyway, like it forgot. I backed the Civic into the last space so the trunk faced the wall. Nobody could walk up behind me. Old habit. The kind the Army puts in you and never takes back out.

I turned the engine off. The heat came in right away, even after dark. It sat on my chest like a second blanket.

I counted the streetlights. Seven along the front of the lot. Two on the side. Nine.

I counted again. Nine.

Good. The numbers were behaving tonight.

My phone said eleven percent. I turned the brightness all the way down and opened my contacts and looked at Emma's name for a while. I didn't call. I never called. I just liked knowing the number still worked, the way you like knowing a door is there even if you'll never open it.

I put the phone face down on the passenger seat.

The watch on my wrist ticked. My father's watch. I could hear it when the lot was quiet, a small steady sound under the hum of the lights. I'd started setting my breathing to it. Four ticks in. Four ticks out. The VA therapist had taught me the breathing. The watch was my idea.

Around midnight a car pulled into the lot.

Headlights swept across the windshield and I was awake all the way, fast, like somebody had thrown cold water on the inside of my skull. The car rolled past the sandwich shop. Slow. It stopped at the far end, under the first streetlight. The buzzing one.

Engine running. Lights off.

I didn't move. Moving is how people see you.

I tried to read the shape. Sedan. Dark color. Dark windows, or maybe just dark, because everything was dark. I couldn't see a driver. I couldn't see anything except the faint orange from the lamp sliding over the roof.

Nobody got out.

Four ticks in. Four ticks out.

I told myself the reasonable things. Somebody's waiting for a friend. Somebody's on the phone and doesn't want to do it at home. Somebody's lost and checking a map. People sit in parked cars all the time. I was sitting in a parked car. That didn't make me a threat. It made me tired.

The doctors had a word for what my brain did. They had a lot of words. Hypervigilance was one. It meant my head was a smoke detector that went off when you made toast. It meant I couldn't trust the alarm.

So I didn't trust it. I watched the car anyway.

Ten minutes. Fifteen.

The sedan didn't leave. The OPEN sign flickered once and came back. A plane crossed the sky, blinking red, low and slow.

I picked up the phone without turning it over. I wanted the weight of it in my hand. Eleven percent was enough for one call. I ran through who it would be. Not the cops. The cops would look at the garbage bags in my back seat and the sleeping bag and the empty bottles and decide which one of us was the problem. Not Emma. Not my father.

That was the list. That was the whole list.

At twelve thirty-one, by my father's watch, the sedan's brake lights came on. Red across the asphalt. Then off. Then the car rolled forward, slow, all the way down the row toward me.

It passed close. Close enough that I could have touched the paint if my window had been open. I didn't look at it. I looked at my own hands on the steering wheel. They were shaking. They always shook now.

The car turned out onto the road and the sound of it went away, and the lot was just the lot again. Hum. Buzz. Tick.

I sat there until my heart came down.

Then I did the thing I'd started doing, the thing I didn't tell anyone about. I opened the glove compartment and took out the pen I kept there and wrote on the back of a gas receipt.

12:04. Dark sedan. Far end. Lights off. Nobody out.

12:31. Left. Drove past me.

I looked at what I'd written. In the dark it didn't look like much. Two lines. A crazy man's grocery list.

But in the morning I'd forget. That was the part nobody understood. In the morning the whole thing would be gone, or it would be changed, or I'd remember it as a dream. The receipt would still say what it said. Paper doesn't have a brain injury.

I folded it and put it in the glove compartment with the others.

There were a lot of others.

I lay back across the seat and tucked the sleeping bag under my head. The watch ticked. The streetlights hummed. I counted them one more time to be sure.

Nine.

Then ten.

I sat up.

Then nine again, and I lay back down, and I told myself it was the brain, it was only ever the brain, and I watched the far end of the lot until the sky went gray.

microbooks.title: Pump Six
microbooks.pov: Teo, an original overnight gas station clerk
microbooks.when: An unspecified night in HUNTED's world
microbooks.setting_mood: gas station canopy at 2 AM, a man asleep in an old Honda, a clean black sedan
microbooks.logline: An overnight clerk notices a black sedan at pump six that never buys gas, and a notebook pointed at the old Honda in the far corner.
microbooks.canon_notes: Original side character. Teo is 23 so he is not the hostile teenage clerk from HUNTED Chapter 1. The man in the Honda is never named. The watcher is never named or explained.
microbooks.label: Original companion fiction set in the world of the Ryan Kane Series. Not an excerpt from any book.
microbooks.text:
The overnight shift at the station had three rules, and Teo had written none of them.

Don't leave the register. Don't open the door after two unless it's a cop. Don't get involved.

He was twenty-three and four months into the job, and he had gotten very good at the third one.

At one in the morning the store was all hum. The coolers hummed. The lights hummed. The hot dog roller turned the same four hot dogs it had been turning since ten. Outside, the canopy lit the pumps like a stage, and past the edge of the light the lot went dark fast, as if somebody had cut it with scissors.

There was an old Honda parked out there in the dark. Far corner, by the air pump that didn't work. It had been there three nights in a row.

Teo knew the type. Everybody who worked nights knew the type. Somebody sleeping in their car. Usually they came in once, used the bathroom, bought nothing or bought one coffee and made it last. Usually they were gone by six. His manager said to call it in if they stayed past a week.

This one hadn't come in at all. That was the strange part. Teo had seen him only once, walking back to the Honda with a gallon of water from somewhere else, a tall guy with his shoulders up near his ears like it was cold. It wasn't cold. It was never cold.

At 1:14 a black sedan pulled in under the canopy and stopped at pump six.

Nice car. Clean. Dark windows. The kind of car that doesn't need gas at a place like this, because the kind of person who drives it gets gas somewhere with a car wash and good coffee.

Nobody got out.

Teo waited for pump six to light up on his screen. Pay at the pump, or prepay inside. Neither happened. Pump six just sat there, idle, with the black car beside it like a dog sitting next to a bowl it had no plan to eat from.

He rang up a guy buying cigarettes and a lottery ticket. He said have a good night. He looked up again.

Still there.

From the register he could see the driver's side, and the window was down maybe two inches. Not enough to see a face. Enough for a thin line of light from a phone screen. Then the light went away and something else moved, slow and careful. A hand holding a pen. A small notebook resting on the steering wheel.

Writing.

Teo followed where the windshield was pointed.

The far corner. The Honda.

He told himself it could be anything. A repo guy. An insurance thing. A private investigator, which Teo knew about only from TV, but still. Somebody checking up on somebody. People wrote things down. That wasn't a crime.

But the sedan had parked at pump six, and pump six had the best view of the far corner. He'd never thought about that before. Now he couldn't stop thinking about it.

At 1:40 the Honda's dome light came on. Just for a second. Teo saw the shape of the guy sitting up, one hand pressed flat to the side of his head, the way you'd hold a door shut against the wind. Then the light went off again.

In the sedan, the pen moved.

Teo's phone was in his back pocket. He took it out and held it under the counter where the camera couldn't see, which was stupid, since nobody watched the footage unless something got stolen. He opened the keypad.

What would he say? There's a car at my pump that isn't buying gas. There's a man sleeping in my lot who hasn't stolen anything. There's somebody writing in a notebook.

He could hear how it would sound. He could hear the dispatcher's voice, polite and tired.

He put the phone back.

At 2:10 the sedan's engine turned over, smooth and quiet, and it rolled out from under the canopy. It didn't take the exit to the street. It went the long way, around the back of the lot, past the dumpsters, and slow along the dark edge where the Honda sat. Slow enough that Teo held his breath. Then out the side driveway and gone.

The Honda didn't move.

At six, when his shift ended, Teo did something he had never done in four months. He bought a bottle of water with his own money and walked it out to the far corner of the lot.

The guy was asleep, folded across the front seat. Garbage bags in the back. The windows fogged a little from his breathing. Teo stood there with the water in his hand, feeling dumb, feeling like he should knock and not wanting to.

He set the bottle on the hood instead, where the guy would see it.

On the way back to his own car he passed pump six. There was something on the ground beside it. A small square of paper, torn from a notebook, pinned under the edge of the island where the wind had pushed it.

He picked it up.

It was just numbers. Times. 1:14. 1:40. 2:10. And next to 1:40, two words in small, neat handwriting.

Still awake.

Teo looked at the Honda. Then at the street. Then at his own hands, which he noticed were not quite steady.

He put the paper in his pocket. He did not throw it away. He did not call anyone, either.

Nobody ever looks, his manager liked to say. That's what makes night shift easy.

Teo had always thought it was a joke.

microbooks.title: Last Run
microbooks.pov: Marisol, an original night bus driver
microbooks.setting_mood: last bus of the night, rain, a sedan stopping at every stop
microbooks.logline: A bus driver on the last run of the night realizes a black sedan is stopping every time she does.
microbooks.canon_notes: Original characters only. The rider is not Ryan (he has no car and sleeps behind a hospital). City unnamed. Echoes the series theme of invisible people without adding canon.
microbooks.label: Original companion fiction set in the world of the Ryan Kane Series. Not an excerpt from any book.
microbooks.text:
Marisol drove the last run of the night, the one that left the transit center at eleven fifty and came back around one, mostly empty.

She liked it. People thought she was crazy for liking it. But the last run was quiet, and the city at that hour belonged to the people who had nowhere else to be, and she had spent enough years with nowhere else to be that she didn't mind their company.

There was a man who got on at the stop outside the closed furniture store. Same stop every night for two weeks. Hard to say how old. Clean jacket that didn't fit right, like it came from a donation bin. He always paid in exact change, coins counted out in his palm before the doors even opened. He always sat in the first sideways seat, the one facing the aisle, with his back against the window.

Not facing forward. Not facing back. Facing the door.

Marisol had a brother who sat like that in restaurants. She didn't ask the man about it.

He rode to the end of the line every night and walked off toward the parking lots behind the hospital. She figured he slept somewhere out there. She figured that was his business.

On the Thursday it rained, which it almost never did, she noticed the car.

Black sedan. It was behind the bus when she pulled away from the furniture store. That wasn't strange. Cars got stuck behind buses all the time. They honked, they swerved around, they cursed you out the window.

This one didn't swerve around.

At the next stop she pulled to the curb and opened the doors, and nobody got on, and nobody got off, and in her side mirror the sedan pulled to the curb too. Twenty feet back. Headlights on. Wipers going.

She closed the doors. Pulled out. The sedan pulled out.

Next stop. Same thing.

She looked in the big mirror over the windshield, the one that showed her the whole inside of the bus. Three riders. A woman asleep against the window in a grocery store uniform. A kid with headphones. And the man in the sideways seat, very still.

He wasn't watching the door anymore. He was watching the back window. He'd seen it too.

Their eyes met in the mirror. He looked away first.

At the fifth stop Marisol did something she wasn't supposed to do. She didn't pull to the curb. She stopped in the lane, hazards on, opened the front door, and waited.

Behind her, the sedan stopped too. It had nowhere to go. There was a parked truck on its right and the bus in front of it, and for a second she felt good, felt clever, like she had caught something by the tail.

Then the sedan's driver's window came down.

Not all the way. A few inches. She couldn't see a face. Rain, and the glare of headlights in her mirror, and the dark inside the car. But a hand came out, palm up, and caught a little rain, the way you would if you were checking whether it was still coming down.

Then the hand went back in and the window went up.

It was a nothing gesture. It was the most normal thing in the world. It made the back of her neck go cold.

She closed the door and drove.

At the next light the sedan turned right and was gone, smooth, signal on, like any car on any road on any night. Marisol watched the empty mirror for three more stops.

At the end of the line the woman in the grocery uniform woke up and got off, and the kid with the headphones got off, and the man in the sideways seat stood but didn't move toward the door.

"You saw it," he said.

It wasn't a question. His voice was low and careful, like he was setting something fragile on a table.

"I saw a car," Marisol said.

He nodded. He looked down at his hands. They were shaking a little, and he pressed them flat against his legs to stop it.

"Okay," he said. "Okay. Thank you."

"For what?"

He didn't answer right away. He thought about it. She could see him thinking about it.

"For saying it was there," he said.

Then he got off the bus and walked into the rain toward the dark lots behind the hospital, and he didn't look back, and she didn't watch him go, because she'd been raised to think that watching somebody walk away was a kind of rudeness.

The next night he wasn't at the stop outside the furniture store.

Or the night after that.

She told her supervisor about the sedan, finally, and her supervisor asked if the car had hit the bus, and she said no, and he asked if anybody had been hurt, and she said no, and he asked what exactly she wanted him to write down.

She didn't have an answer for that.

She still drives the last run. She still looks at the stop outside the furniture store, every night, out of habit. Sometimes there's someone there. Sometimes they sit facing the door.

She always waits a little longer than she has to before she pulls away.

microbooks.title: The Log
microbooks.logline: Seven days of notes kept by someone watching a man who lives in his car.
microbooks.canon_notes: Builds on the approved HUNTED blurb line "Somebody is keeping a log on him" and the book's open scenes of a man watching from a sedan. Watcher is unnamed. No names, motives, plans or later events are revealed.
microbooks.label: Original companion fiction set in the world of the Ryan Kane Series. Not an excerpt from any book.
microbooks.text:
These pages were never meant to be read by the man they describe.

DAY 1

06:12. Subject awake. Sits up slowly. Holds right side of head for approx. 40 seconds.

06:20. Exits vehicle. Checks all four door handles before walking away. Checks driver's door twice.

06:31. Gas station restroom. Nine minutes.

06:44. Returns. Buys nothing.

07:02. Sitting in vehicle. Counting something. Lips moving. Fingers tapping the steering wheel.

Note: He counts things. Find out what.

DAY 2

05:58. Awake early. Dome light on at 02:15 and again at 03:40. Did not sleep well.

06:30. Walks the lot perimeter before restroom. Looks at every parked car. Does not look at this one.

09:10. Sits on curb in shade. Takes out phone. Looks at screen for four minutes. No call placed.

Note: There is a number he does not call. Find out whose.

13:00. Heat. Subject moves vehicle twelve feet to follow the shade of one tree. Gets out, checks handles, gets back in.

Note: Not lazy. Not careless. Tired in a way that looks like careless from a distance. People who walk past him see careless. That is useful.

DAY 3

06:05. Awake.

06:06. Stares at the glove compartment for a long time. Opens it. Takes out a piece of paper. Writes on it. Puts it back.

Note: He writes things down too.

Note: Find out what he writes.

11:20. Subject drops keys twice trying to unlock door. Hands not steady. Sits on the ground beside the car for six minutes with his eyes shut.

11:26. Stands. Tries again. Succeeds.

Note: He does not ask anyone for help. Three people walked past during those six minutes. None of them stopped.

Nobody stops. That is the whole point.

DAY 4

No entries before noon. Subject did not leave vehicle.

12:15. Exits. Walks toward the road. Stops at the edge of the lot. Turns around. Comes back.

Note: He wanted to go somewhere and could not decide where. Or he forgot where. The difference matters. Find out which.

16:45. Subject looks directly at this vehicle.

Eleven seconds.

Does not approach. Does not write it down. Goes back to his car and sits with both hands flat on the wheel.

Note: He notices more than he believes he notices. That is the thing to understand about him. The alarm in his head goes off all the time, so he has trained himself not to listen to it. He will see you and then talk himself out of having seen you.

Recommend more distance anyway.

DAY 5

Changed vehicles.

06:10. Subject awake. Same routine. Handles. Restroom. Counting.

07:30. Two young men argue near the ice machine. Loud. One shoves the other. Subject is out of his car before the second shove lands. Not running. Not shouting. Standing between them with his hands open at his sides.

They stop.

They leave.

Subject stands there after they go, breathing hard, looking at his own hands as if they belong to someone else.

Note: Still has the training. Still moves toward trouble when anyone else would move away. He thinks that part of him is gone. It isn't. It is just buried under everything else.

Note: That part is worth a great deal.

DAY 6

03:00. Light rain. Rare. Subject awake, watching it run down the windshield.

03:20. He has his forehead against the glass.

Note: Nothing to record.

Note: Recording it anyway.

DAY 7

06:12. Awake.

06:20. Handles. Driver's door twice.

06:31. Restroom. Nine minutes.

Note: Same as Day 1. To the minute, almost. A life folded down to the size of a parking space. He does not know how small it has gotten. Nobody has told him. Nobody is around to tell him.

Note: Someone will be.

Last entry for this week. The rule stands. Never the same car twice in one day. Never close enough to be sure of. Let him wonder.

Wondering is the part that wears a person down.

microbooks.title: Vacancy
microbooks.pov: Lorna, an original motel night clerk
microbooks.setting_mood: motel at the edge of town, half dead sign, room fourteen
microbooks.logline: A motel night clerk writes a license plate on her wrist when a black sedan parks across from room fourteen.
microbooks.canon_notes: Original characters. The guest is never named. Nothing in it confirms or contradicts any HUNTED scene.
microbooks.label: Original companion fiction set in the world of the Ryan Kane Series. Not an excerpt from any book.
microbooks.text:
The sign out front said VACANCY in red letters, except the V had been dead since summer, so at night it said ACANCY, and Lorna had stopped noticing.

She worked the desk from ten to six at a two-story motel near the edge of town, the kind with outdoor stairs and an ice machine that groaned like an animal every forty minutes. People paid by the night. Some paid by the week. Lorna didn't ask anybody why. In her experience, nobody who checked in at midnight wanted to be asked why.

At 11:40 a man came in.

He stood just inside the glass door for a second before he walked up to the counter, the way people do when they're letting their eyes adjust. Or the way people do when they're checking who else is in the room. There was nobody else in the room. There was Lorna, and the coffee pot nobody drank from, and the little TV on the wall playing a cooking show with the sound off.

"How much for one night?"

She told him. He nodded, took out a fold of bills, and counted them on the counter. Then he counted them again. His lips moved the second time.

"Ground floor," he said. "If you have it. Facing the lot."

"So you can see your car?"

He looked at her for a moment like she'd read his mind. Then he almost smiled. "Yeah."

She gave him fourteen. She slid the key across. He picked it up, and then he didn't leave.

"Has anybody asked about me?" he said.

Lorna blinked. "You just got here."

"Right." He rubbed the side of his head, just above his right ear, like something hurt there. "Right. Sorry. Long day."

"Long night," she said, and he did smile at that, a little, before he went out.

At 2:05 a black sedan pulled into the lot.

Lorna saw it on the camera monitor first, a gray shape on a gray screen, and then she looked up through the glass door and saw it for real. It parked across from the ground floor rooms. Right across from fourteen. Lights off. Engine running. She could see the faint exhaust in the cold air.

Nobody got out.

Nobody came to the desk.

People pulled into motel lots at two in the morning for a lot of reasons. Lorna had seen most of them. Somebody waiting for somebody. Somebody too drunk to drive the last mile home and smart enough to know it. Somebody making a phone call they didn't want anyone to hear.

Has anybody asked about me?

She didn't want to think about that. She thought about it anyway.

The notepad was at the far end of the counter, and she didn't want to move, didn't want the motion to show through the glass. So she picked up the pen and wrote the plate on the inside of her own wrist, the way she used to write phone numbers in high school. She had to squint. The sign above the lot only lit half of it. She got the letters. She got most of the numbers.

At 2:40 the sedan backed out, slow, and pulled onto the road and was gone.

Across the lot, the curtain in fourteen moved. Just an inch. A sliver of a face. Then the curtain went still.

He'd been awake the whole time. Of course he had.

At 5:30, before the sky even started to go pale, the man from fourteen came back to the desk with the key. He'd showered. His hair was wet. He looked like he hadn't slept at all.

Lorna took the key. She thought about not saying anything. That was the rule, the one nobody wrote down. You don't get involved.

"There was a car out there last night," she said.

He went very still. "Black?"

"Yeah."

"You saw it?" He said it carefully, like the answer mattered more than the question. "You actually saw it."

"I saw it. I didn't see the driver."

He let out a breath that seemed to come from somewhere very deep. "I thought maybe I dreamed it," he said. "I do that sometimes."

"I wrote down the plate." She turned her wrist over to show him.

They both looked at it.

The ink had smeared. Her own skin, her own sleeve, an hour of rubbing at her wrist without noticing. The letters were still there. The numbers were a blur. A seven, maybe. Or a one. Maybe a four that had lost its top.

She felt stupid. She started to apologize.

"It's okay," he said. He was still looking at her wrist. "The numbers do that to me too."

Then he thanked her, and he went out to his car, and he checked every door handle before he got in, and he drove away. She watched him turn onto the road in the same direction the sedan had gone.

She washed her wrist in the bathroom sink at the end of her shift. Then she stood there with the water running, looking at her clean skin, trying to remember the plate.

She couldn't.

The next night the V was still dead. ACANCY. She noticed it for the first time in months.

picks.tagline: Some cities die from neglect. Others are murdered on purpose.
picks.blurb: Some cities die from neglect. Others are murdered on purpose. Detective Malloy has spent her career holding East Baltimore together with sheer will. Now the deaths are coming faster, overdoses, stabbings, and disappearances with too many questions and not enough answers. Beside her stand Officers Nia Wallace and Ryan Mitchell, two allies she can still trust when every other badge feels compromised. Together they follow a trail of falsified reports, silent witnesses, and redevelopment plans built on blood. Across the block, Hattie Carter searches for her missing grandson, and Darius, a boy desperate to be the hero, dives headfirst into a rescue that may cost him everything. As their worlds collide, Malloy discovers that the city's rebirth is a performance staged for power. The real story hides in the shadows, where truth is rewritten, loyalty is a weapon, and hope is the hardest thing to save.

picks.title: Stalker
picks.author: Tom Claren
picks.tagline: Someone tries to kill my best friend. I vow to track them down.
picks.blurb: Someone tries to kill my best friend. I vow to track them down. When a truck rams our car on a dark country road, everyone calls it a terrible accident. I know better, because my best friend Mia has been hiding the fact that she has a stalker. I'm a medical student. I trust evidence over excuses, and every clue I uncover points to a predator willing to destroy anyone who stands in his way. The deeper I dig, the more the local police dismiss my fears. Powerful people close ranks, and I realize the cover-up may be as dangerous as the crime itself. Then the stalker turns his attention to me. Now I'm being hunted by someone who believes fear will keep me silent. To save my best friend and expose the truth, I must outthink a ruthless killer before his obsession becomes my death sentence.

picks.title: Garden Of Lies
picks.author: Jemma Stark
picks.tagline: A high-profile death. A city full of secrets.
picks.blurb: A billionaire is found dead in New Orleans, and the case is ruled a suicide. The governor isn't buying it. Special Agents Briana Song and James Buckley dig into the tycoon's high-society world and find enemies everywhere, and lies at every turn. To uncover the truth, Briana starts bending the rules, and puts herself directly in the killer's sights. Accident or murder? Truth or lies? In the Garden District, nothing is what it seems.

picks.title: The Empty Boat
picks.author: Natasha Stone
picks.kicker: A Haunting Domestic Suspense Psychological Thriller · The "Empty" Thriller Series, Book 9
picks.tagline: Some secrets can destroy a marriage. Others can destroy everything.
picks.blurb: Some secrets can destroy a marriage. Others can destroy everything. Alyssa is looking forward to a relaxing Fourth of July weekend with her husband Keith, her younger sister Mandi, and Mandi's husband Greg. Their beautiful vacation home on a secluded South Carolina island seems like the perfect escape from everyday life. But as soon as they arrive, Alyssa learns something that changes everything. Mandi has been having an affair with a local charter boat captain. Worse, she has no intention of leaving her husband. She expects Alyssa to keep her secret, even as the four of them spend the weekend together. Now Alyssa is caught between loyalty to her sister and the burden of keeping a secret that could tear their families apart. Every conversation feels uncomfortable, and every smile hides another lie. Then, after a tense Saturday night, Mandi disappears. And the longer Mandi is missing, the more Alyssa wonders what else her sister has been hiding. THE EMPTY BOAT is Book 9 of The "Empty" Thriller Series. It can be read as a standalone.

picks.title: THEIRS
picks.author: Liz Sinclair
picks.tagline: Eleanor Adler is dead. And her daughter-in-law is relieved.
picks.blurb: Eleanor Adler is dead. And her daughter-in-law is relieved. For thirteen years, Eleanor has interfered in Hannah's marriage and parenting. No matter how often Hannah said no, Eleanor never listened. Now Eleanor lies dead at the foot of her staircase. Hannah should finally be free of her. Instead, the police suspect foul play. The front door was unlocked. Eleanor may have survived her fall for over an hour. And someone is lying about the night she died. The investigation begins to expose secrets Hannah never imagined. Her sister-in-law threatened to keep Eleanor from her own grandchild. A man with a restraining order in his past lied about visiting her. Even Eleanor's devoted husband is hiding something. The more Hannah learns about Eleanor's final days, the less she can walk away. She wanted Eleanor out of her life. Now, buried in her family's secrets, she may never escape what Eleanor left behind.
